input.title: 117 Days of Silence, and the Way Back
input.text_summary: Rep. Tom Kean Jr. returned to the House floor on 2026-07-07 after a 117-day absence during which he missed votes and offered no public explanation, drawing speculation. In his return remarks he disclosed he had been hospitalized for clinical depression. He did not explain his way back; he spoke his way back. Source: Democracy Now! headlines, 2026-07-07.

sequence.phrase: 117 days of silence — a private collapse, hidden
the hinge: he stops hiding and starts searching for what's still good in himself
searches and gathers the good points still in himself
opens back into prayer — he can speak again
Rebbe Nachman's charge: carry this teaching, always
the wider principle: judge any person favorably by finding the good in him
raising him from guilt to merit, until he returns
and so too, a person must find this also in himself

narrative:
For 117 days, a congressman simply vanished — missed votes, no explanation, the kind of silence that lets people assume the worst. Colleagues wondered if he'd quit on them. He hadn't. He'd been hospitalized for clinical depression, ashamed enough to disappear rather than say so.

Then he stood on the House floor and said it anyway.

That return traces an old path. An 18th-century Hasidic teacher, Rebbe Nachman, built a teaching around this exact moment — a person looking inward and finding nothing good to say for himself. Search anyway, he teaches. Find one point that's still good. Then another. Gather them, and — startlingly — they become song: the small good still in you turns into something you can sing. That joy opens a person back into prayer, and from there, the teaching goes, he can be brought all the way back.

To my eye, the same move runs underneath: judge people favorably by hunting for the bit of good even in someone who looks entirely lost — then turn that same hunt on yourself.

The way back rarely starts when the darkness lifts. It starts when you find the little in yourself still worth speaking for — and speak. Tonight, name one thing you did right today, out loud, to one person who'll hear it.
